title: Whither shall I flee?
hookLine: if I take the wings of the morning, even there (Psalm 139)
tomorrow: a psalm with wild goats, lions and a sea monster at play. why?

lines: A STORM, A SEA, A FISH.
cards: Jonah gets a call from God to go to Nineveh, and he goes down to the port instead.
The book of Jonah says he rose up "to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD," and paid the fare, as if God's presence stopped at the dock.
Then a storm, a crew throwing cargo overboard, Jonah thrown into the sea, and a great fish. And from inside the fish, Jonah prays. So what was waiting at the edge of the map?
The one he ran from. Psalm 139 has an odd way of saying that: it lists hiding places like someone checking every exit.

teach.b: The psalm asks, "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?" Then the list.
"If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there." Hell here is the Hebrew Sheol, the place of the dead. Up as far as up goes, down as far as down goes.

teach.h: A HAND THAT LEADS AND HOLDS.
teach.b: Then across: "If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; Even there shall thy hand lead me, and thy right hand shall hold me." Here's the puzzle.
Read cold, this sounds like surveillance: nowhere to hide. But look at the hand at the end of the list. It doesn't grab; it leads and holds.
And the psalm opens, "O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me." Known all the way down, and held anyway.
That's the teaching Jews and Christians draw from it: God is present everywhere, so no ship, no sea and no grave is out of reach. Jonah learned it the hard way.
One to tell a friend: Jewish tradition reads the book of Jonah on the afternoon of Yom Kippur, a story about a man who couldn't outrun God, read on the day people come back.
And the psalm's own answer to its puzzle is a few lines on: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made."

how: Psalm 139 is prayed by Jews and Christians as a psalm of being known by God; in synagogues the book of Jonah is read on the afternoon of Yom Kippur.

games.q: what does “whither shall i flee?” mean?
o: a prophet's plea to be taken off a sinking ship
a soldier's prayer before running from a lost battle
a psalm's question: where could I go to get away from God?

games.q: the runaway and the psalm: tap the pairs.
p: the Hebrew place of the dead
even there, a hand to hold

s: Psalm 139 is about God catching people who try to hide
the hand at the end of the list leads and holds, and the psalm turns to praise: fearfully and wonderfully made.
Jewish tradition reads the book of Jonah on Yom Kippur
on the afternoon of the Day of Atonement: a runaway, read on the day people come back.
'hell' in this psalm is the Hebrew word Sheol
the place of the dead: down as far as down goes, and thou art there.

games.q: your friend's grandmother is moving into a care home far from her old church, and she's afraid God won't find her there. what would Psalm 139 say?
o: there's no place too far: even there shall thy hand lead me.
she'll be fine as soon as she finds a new church nearby.
it says no one can hide from God's judgment, wherever they go.
games.why: the psalm's list of far places ends in a hand that leads and holds, at the uttermost parts of the sea.

practice: Close your eyes and sit as you are, not as you'd like to be seen. Let one true thing about today come to mind, a worry or a mistake, and don't fix it. Just let it be fully known, and keep breathing.

wordCard.voice: Whither shall I flee? The psalm's question with no exit: not heaven, not Sheol, not the far sea, and a hand there to hold.

orig.note: Hebrew, Psalm 139:9: wings of the dawn, the KJV's wings of the morning.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: the wings of the morning still land in a hand that holds. The hills yesterday, the far sea today: this psalm travels too.
